A witness to the deadly shooting inside a Halloween store at a Bay Area mall described the terrifying scene as shots rang out and she ducked for cover — fearing she was “going to die” as several victims were struck by gunfire.

Jocelyn Lopez Tabares, 15, and her 23-year-old sister were picking up last-minute accessories for their costumes Friday night at the Spirit Halloween store at the Solano Town Center in Fairfield when a barrage of shots erupted.

“I felt like I was going to die,” Lopez Tabares, of Vallejo, told the California Post. “I thought it was going to be my last time living. I didn’t want to die that way.”

The shooting, which left one person dead and six others injured, was a “targeted incident” carried out by a lone gunman, police announced. The suspect remained on the run as of Saturday afternoon.

Lopez Tabares, who was standing near the checkout registers, initially mistook the gunfire for popping balloons, until her sister dragged her to the concrete floor, she recalled

“We were in line getting ready to leave,” Lopez Tabares said. “Out of nowhere, we just hear at least 10 shots go off. I thought it was a balloon popping. I was in shock, and everyone just went down. My sister pulled me down because I couldn’t move. I was so scared.”

As dozens of shoppers scrambled toward the exits in panic, the 15-year-old found herself frozen on the floor.

The teen then pulled out her cellphone and began recording, determined to document the scene in case she did not survive.

Protesters interrupted him multiple times, and each time, he became more visibly agitated. “Shut up. Shut up. Dope. Shut up, loser,” he barked at one of them, before adding, “These guys are losers. It’s always at my punchline.” He claimed, like he always does, that they were “paid by Soros” for $250 each and that his team had their names. The reality is that they are not being paid, and more and more people are protesting because they know how important it is to do so. Now, night after night, in front of the cameras and his most loyal supporters, he is seeing for himself that even the people who once made him feel untouchable can no longer shield him from the growing resistance to his presidency.

July | Online Community

This is more than a book club. This is a structured anti-racism learning space created by Day and Brandi for white women who are ready to learn, unlearn, reflect, and take action.

For nearly 2 years, this community has grown to more than 150 members. Together, members read one book each month, join monthly discussions, watch documentaries and TED Talks, complete reflection work, and participate in deeper conversations that move beyond surface-level learning.

The program is $22 per month, about $5.50 per week. Scholarships are available for members who cannot afford the monthly membership fee.

The 3-year journey includes:

Year 1: Actor Level
Identify performative actions, uncover new ways to raise awareness, and begin the internal work.

Year 2: Ally Level
Deepen your education, amplify Black voices, and learn how to leverage privilege for advocacy.

Year 3: Accomplice Level
Use your privilege to actively fight racism and injustice through real action.

Members also receive tools for deeper learning, including journaling prompts, conversation starters, quarterly quizzes, a private Facebook group, monthly orientation meetings, yearly in-person events, quarterly fireside chats, and special conversations.

This space is led by Black women and designed specifically for white women because white women are uniquely positioned to challenge racism in their homes, workplaces, friendships, and communities.

Join the club: bookclubs.com/anti-racism-book-club-13/join/
Or click the link in my bio.

Scholarship information: AntiRacismscholarship@gmail.com
Questions: antiracismbookclub1@gmail.com

Learn more about me: www.iamdaymadison.com

Follow my pages @realblackgirlpolitics and @dearwhitepeople.lets.talk for more anti-racism education.

Utah has a coal plant that was never allowed to die. The coal units at the Intermountain Power Project near Delta stopped running last year when new gas units took over, so the lights never went out. But the Legislature passed a law blocking anyone from decommissioning them. They’ve been kept in working order, like a truck on blocks, waiting for a buyer.

On November 4, a committee picks that buyer from four secret bids. Every bidder signed a nondisclosure agreement, and state officials confirmed to lawmakers that the public can’t see a single offer. The state gets the final say, and it can even buy the coal units itself with your money.

Who wants a 40-year-old coal plant? At least one data center developer in Delta has said publicly it wants these units to power a giant AI campus. That campus has one small tenant and is hunting for big ones. If no big customer shows up, nobody restarts the coal.

So here’s my question for OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, Google, Amazon and xAI. You’ve all promised that AI won’t run on dirty power or on the backs of families’ electric bills. Will you commit, in public, not to lease computing at any campus powered by a restarted coal plant? Yes or no. Silence counts as an answer.

Share this with one person who works in tech, because their inbox matters more than mine. And follow along, because on November 4 we find out who wins the secret bid.

Nobody told us. We found out from the maps they gave Salt Lake City.

Here’s what HF Sinclair told its investors: the fuel is for Nevada and California. Utah is the hallway. They get the profit. We get the trench, the risk, and the cleanup when it leaks. And pipelines leak. In 2010, oil ran into Red Butte Creek for about ten hours before anyone noticed.

Now think about what Utah just lived through. The lowest snowpack ever recorded. Resorts opened late and closed early. Skier days fell by a quarter and Summit County took the biggest tourism-tax hit in the state. People here lost whole seasons of income. And the state’s answer is to fast-track more fossil fuel infrastructure through our drinking water?

They already have a pipeline corridor down Weber Canyon. They could upgrade it. That would mean a few months of downtime. A new line through our neighborhoods means they never miss a dollar.

Who decides? Not us. The Legislature passed a law this year to speed up pipeline permits, and Summit County can’t veto the route.

Our water is not a shortcut for HF Sinclair’s record profits.

I received the first copies of the newly reissued Yes Symphonic Live album on vinyl, CD, and Blu-ray featuring my illustrations. Street date 1/23/26. I wrote the following for the liner notes:

“For the new cover art, I reimagined (or “magnified”) my original 2002 Symphonic Live cover. In this new edition, we see a prehistoric shaman summoning a Talisman’s power above a vast forest – the energy of its levitating rings opening crop circle style sinkholes in the ground. 

I also created an “alternate cover” that’s a little more intimate, depicting a man and his child watching as a Talisman’s silver rings return to sacred ground overlooking a hazy canyon. As an homage to the great album artist Aubrey “Po” Powell, who masterfully directed the Symphonic Live concert film, I chose to bring back the Hipgnosis treatment of Roger Dean’s Yes logo last seen on the covers of Going For The One and Tormato.

Elsewhere, the gatefold illustration shows four colossal Talisman monuments relaying bolts of energy to open a dimensional rift. Another illustration, “Giant Under The Sun”, is a tribute to Chris Squire, featuring a humpback whale rejoicing before a massive oceanic Talisman.

Late in the process, I decided to have some fun bridging the ancient and modern eras of interdimensional reality, so I created an archival photograph of an early 20th Century explorer’s discovery of a Talisman while it’s partially exposed by melting ice, adapting a public domain photograph by Herbert G. Ponting, circa 1911.

One final note: every composition in this sleeve was modeled, composited, or digitally hand-drawn by me, except for the aforementioned Ponting photo. None of the illustrations were created using AI. However, I used Photoshop’s generative tools to clean-up and composite some of the CG renders.

Thank you to everyone at Mercury Studios for gifting me with the rare privilege of working on this special edition of Symphonic Live, and to Jordan Berliant for initially commissioning my work back in 2001-2002. I’m especially grateful for the support of the Yes fan community.”

Long story short… The PACT Act was a law signed by Biden on 8/10/22 and is viewed as the most significant expansion of VA benefits in decades. It’s short for Sergeant First Class (SFC) Health Robinson Honoring Our Promise to Address Comprehensive Toxics Act of 2022. 

It provides new and expanded benefits for Vets (and their survivors) exposed to burn pits and other toxic substances. Benefits of the PACT Act include: 
- Expanded access to VA health care 
- New and expanded presumptive conditions
- Increased compensation for service-connected disabilities
- New and expanded benefits for survivors. 

The VA offers a simple and easy to read visual to understand which route to apply is best for you (or your loved one). Check our link in bio to access this doc!

- Walk-In to your local care provider: VA.gov/find/locations 
- Ask your local VA org for help (VA.gov/disability/get-help-filing-claim)

- Your medical records may become more difficult to obtain. 
- Your condition may worsen over time. This could make it more difficult to prove your disability.

#2 - Prepare your documentation
Don't skip getting a medical opinion, it can help strengthen your case
- Make a copy of your DD-214 (Certificate of Release or Discharge from Active Duty)
- Collect all relevant medical records, both military and civilian
- Gather a statement from a medical professional or other expert attesting to the nature and severity of your disability (Don’t forget about mental health claims if needed, your brain health matters too)

#3 - Common Mistakes and how to avoid them
Mistakes
- Incomplete, insufficient and/or incorrect docs
- Missing deadlines 
- Lack of medical evidence
- Quitting after your claim is denied

How to avoid them
- Incomplete, insufficient and/or incorrect docs
- Missing deadlines 
- Lack of medical evidence
- Quitting after your claim is denied

#4 - Seek professional assistance
Services
- Helping you to understand which benefits you are eligible for
- Helping you gather and organize your evidence
- Reviewing your claim form and providing feedback
- Representing you before the VA during the claims process
- Appealing a denied claim

Benefits
- Increase chances of success
- Reduced stress 
- More time for you to focus on your health and well-being

#5 - Dealing with denials 
- File a Notice of Disagreement (NOD): An NOD is a formal request to the VA to review its decision. 
- Request a Decision Review Officer (DRO) review: A DRO is a VA employee who reviews denied claims and makes recommendations on whether to approve or deny them. 
- Appeal to the Board of Veterans Appeals (BVA): The BVA is a panel of three judges who review denied claims. 
- File a new claim: If you have new evidence, you can file a new claim

Prop 1 could open the state Constitution to a broad rewrite. Prop 2 targets political money from utilities and major government contractors.
Here’s what you need to know before November.

Proposal 1 asks Michigan voters whether they want to call a Constitutional Convention, commonly called a Con-Con, to undertake a general revision of the Michigan Constitution. This question automatically appears on the ballot every 16 years, and Michigan voters have repeatedly declined to call a convention, including in 1978, 1994 and 2010.

And this is not a proposal to fix one outdated sentence or make one narrowly defined change.

A “general revision” means opening Michigan’s foundational governing document to potentially sweeping changes. A convention could revisit provisions dealing with voting and elections, reproductive freedom, civil rights, taxation, property rights, public pensions, collective bargaining, the powers of state government and much more.

That is what makes Proposal 1 so consequential.

Proposal 2 targets a familiar problem in Michigan politics: companies that depend on decisions from state government can also spend money influencing the people making those decisions.

The proposal would restrict certain political contributions from regulated electric and gas utilities, including DTE and Consumers Energy, as well as companies receiving more than $250,000 a year in government contracts. The restrictions would also reach certain executives, board members and others closely connected to those companies.

The argument from supporters is simple: the companies being regulated shouldn’t be financially supporting the politicians responsible for regulating them.

That concern is especially relevant with Michigan’s monopoly utilities, which rely on state regulators for major decisions involving rates and investments while remaining deeply involved in state politics.

[{'caption': '🌐World-renowned economist and public policy expert Jeffrey Sachs has argued that the global order is undergoing a fundamental transformation, with traditional Western dominance giving way to a more multipolar system.

Speaking at a London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE) event hosted by the Huth Initiative for a New Political Economy on 27 October 2026, said the United States and Europe must recognise that “the world as it really is right now” has changed, pointing to expanding middle classes, urbanisation and economic development across the world.

Sachs said “the idea that the United States or the West still somehow runs the show” no longer reflects current realities, warning that a failure to adapt could contribute to greater geopolitical instability. He also criticised what he described as “double standards” in international affairs, arguing that perceptions of exceptionalism can increase tensions between major powers.

A wider geopolitical reading of Sachs’ remarks reflects the broader debate over the transition from a US-led international system towards a more contested and multipolar order. 

The growth of China, India and other emerging economies has challenged longstanding assumptions about Western economic and strategic primacy, while disagreements over sovereignty, military intervention and international rules have intensified debates over the legitimacy of global leadership. 

His comments highlight the risks of misreading shifts in power, particularly as major states compete to shape the future of global governance, security and economic influence.

ℹ️  LSE

📸  Jeffrey D. Sachs, an economist and professor of Sustainable Development at Columbia University, discusses the role of faith in the modern economy during a Sept. 5 event at Fordham University in New York. (CNS photo/courtesy Leo Sorel)

The confrontation reflected the wider diplomatic divide over US-Cuba relations, with Washington and Havana offering opposing explanations for Cuba’s economic challenges. - Supply chains: The statement called for greater transparency, private-sector investment and cooperation on critical minerals, processing and recycling.

[{'caption': 'Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has repeatedly used the phrase “Texas will always stand with Israel” to describe the state’s political and diplomatic posture toward the country. He used the line at the Israeli-American Council’s 2023 national summit and again in proclamations marking the anniversaries of the October 7 Hamas attacks, pairing it with commitments to combat antisemitism and support Jewish communities in Texas. Abbott has also directed millions of dollars in state security grants toward Jewish organizations and has made support for Israel a recurring part of his administration’s public messaging.

That position has also generated legal and political controversy. Abbott’s 2024 executive order directing Texas universities to strengthen enforcement against antisemitism specifically referenced groups such as Students for Justice in Palestine, prompting a federal lawsuit from Muslim and pro-Palestinian advocacy organizations that argued the policy infringed on protected political speech. Mike Flood faced a hostile response at a GOP town hall in Lincoln, Nebraska, after rejecting the idea of Medicare for All. He also questioned whether healthy, working-age adults should receive government-funded coverage, arguing that federal resources are limited and should be focused on people who need assistance most.

That distinction is why supporters often argue Sanders is misunderstood: “socialism” in American political debate is frequently used as shorthand for a much broader range of government programs than Sanders actually proposes. In Gaza, Palestinians continue to face enormous civilian suffering and displacement amid the Israel–Hamas war. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, decades of conflict, armed groups and exploitation have displaced millions. In Sudan, the war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces has produced mass displacement, famine conditions in parts of the country and widespread atrocities.

Human rights cannot be selective. Palestinian lives matter. Congolese lives matter. Sudanese lives matter. Caring about one crisis does not require ignoring another.

Ceasefires. Humanitarian aid. Protection for civilians. Accountability for abuses. Freedom from exploitation and oppression.

Our humanity should never depend on which tragedy is trending.

[{'caption': '🚨 You can report an insurance company to your state’s Insurance Commissioner. And more people need to know this.

When an insurance company denies medically necessary care, delays payment, mishandles a claim, or engages in potentially unfair practices, you don’t have to simply accept the decision.

You can file a complaint with your state’s Insurance Commissioner — the government office responsible for regulating insurance companies and investigating certain consumer complaints.

What can happen when you file a complaint?

➡️ The insurer may be required to respond to the complaint.
➡️ The state may review whether the company followed applicable insurance laws and regulations.
➡️ The investigation may uncover a pattern of unfair practices.
➡️ Depending on the circumstances, the regulator may take further action.

⚠️ Filing a complaint does NOT guarantee that a denial will be overturned or that your claim will be paid. But it creates a formal record and gives regulators an opportunity to examine what happened.

And here’s what I want patients to understand: An insurance company’s decision is not automatically the final word on your healthcare.

Document what happened. Keep your denial letters. Save your correspondence. Understand your appeal rights. And when appropriate, file a complaint.

As a physician and an independent medical practice owner, I believe patients deserve to know that they have options when the system fails them.

Insurance companies should be held accountable to the laws that govern them.

📣 Share this with someone who has ever been told, “Your insurance won’t cover it.”

She’s gone now, we said goodbye yesterday. 

My parents took her around the world on their motorcycles, she loved it more than anything. She could smell everything on a bike. They rode through old growth forests, deserts, along the ocean, and anywhere a road might take them. We were lucky to have a final Christmas with her last year, a brain tumour made things uncertain but she stuck around long enough to see us start our next chapter as a family. She’s been a part of everything, every hard day was easier because of her.

While looking through my photos, I was reminded of a canoe trip we went on in 2020. We had just finished eating lunch and Dori was taking a nap in an afternoon pocket of sun. As she slept, we all went our own ways and left her to rest. Dori woke up slowly from her nap, looked around and became worried. Everybody left. She jumped up and began looking around. Just then, my mom came up from the water, having gone for a swim. Dori ran over to her, barking the whole way. After that, she was glued to my mom, almost as if she had a grudge. I think Dori’s back in Algonquin now, taking a nap with her family around her, letting her guard down because she knows that everything is okay.

Today is National Truth & Reconciliation day, a day to meant to recognize the horrific traumas of Canada’s genocide and ongoing disposition of Indigenous peoples. Given the white nationalist gathering at Kamloops Indian Residential School, I felt compelled to share some images I made there a number of years ago.

For over a century, the Canadian state worked with the Catholic Church to forcefully separate children from their families. These children were re-educated, malnourished, tortured, abused, and many died. The sites of these atrocities are still standing. You needn’t just look overseas or to the history books to see Canada’s participation in colonization.

The white nationalists who gathered at Kamloops are not a fluke, they are the result of an ongoing attempt to delegitimization the violent history of Canadian colonialism and Residential Schools. This viewpoint has morphed from a fringe far right opinion into a commonly held idea among “common sense” conservatives. It is not enough to ignore or consider such thinking as fringe, it must be challenged clearly and swiftly for the survivors and the victims.

We cannot be tempted by forgetfulness. These actions were undertaken by men and women, we cannot forget the feeling of hatred this history makes us feel; we cannot forget the sacrifice. To paraphrase Walter Benjamin’s Theses on The Philosophy of History, these wish to correct this history is nourished by the image of enslaved ancestors rather than that of liberated grandchildren.

We find the remnants of this genocidal legacy in the ground, air, and waters surrounding us. It is a history has not yet been reconciled for.

These images were shot on 800 iso film, meaning they could only be overexposed. In a technical sense, this would be the wrong situation to shoot this kind of extremely light sensitive film. I believe it is the perfect situation to shoot this film stock; to overexpose images of underexposed history.

[{'caption': 'The finger-pointing has begun at Fox News following Democrats’ sweeping victories in Tuesday’s midterm elections. During Wednesday’s episode of The Five, a discussion about Republicans losing control of the House and Senate turned into a debate over whether Congress or President Donald Trump deserved the blame.

Emily Compagno argued that Republicans had wasted nearly two years of controlling Washington. She called Congress “really unproductive,” criticizing lawmakers for taking extended breaks and failing to pass legislation that voters had been promised. But Dana Perino raised a different point: wasn’t it the president’s responsibility to lead Congress and get lawmakers behind his plans?

Former Democratic Congressman Harold Ford Jr. immediately picked up on that question. “And he didn’t. That’s what you’re saying, right?” he asked. Compagno pushed back, insisting Congress had failed. Ford responded that presidents are supposed to set the agenda, arguing that Trump had focused on passing his “One Big Beautiful Bill” without pushing lawmakers to accomplish much else. “And guess what? That’s why he lost the House and Senate,” Ford said.

Compagno continued defending Trump, blaming Republican lawmakers for failing to turn his executive orders into permanent laws. She also acknowledged that younger voters were frustrated with the party and that Americans had felt the financial effects of tariffs without seeing the promised benefits.

The exchange offered a glimpse into the conversations now taking place among Republicans following their election losses. Compagno maintained that Congress had failed the president, Ford argued that the president had failed to lead Congress, and Perino’s question brought Trump’s own responsibility into the discussion.
